01.note: Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tuvi, a wealthy man, were sitting before Shapur, the king of Persia, when an etrog was brought in. The king cut a slice and ate it, cut a slice for Bati bar Tuvi, then stuck the knife into the ground ten times before cutting a slice for Mar Yehuda. Bati bar Tuvi protested that he too was Jewish; the king answered that he was certain Mar Yehuda was careful about Jewish law but not certain about him. Another version has the king say: remember what you did last night.
01.why: The Gemara has just taught that a good knife thrust ten times into hard ground is clean enough for cutting cold food; the king's treatment of the knife shows that very practice.

people.name: Mar Yehuda
people.about: An important figure of the Exilarch's house, whom the king trusts to keep Jewish law.

people.name: Bati bar Tuvi
people.about: A wealthy Jewish man sitting with Mar Yehuda before the king.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The king of Persia, who hosts the two men and cuts the etrog.

terms.meaning: A citron, a fragrant citrus fruit.
Jewish law.

02.note: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua were traveling by ship. The voyage ran long, Rabban Gamliel's bread ran out, and he lived on the flour Rabbi Yehoshua had brought, explaining that a star rising once in seventy years misleads sailors. Amazed that so wise a man had to sail for a living, Rabban Gamliel heard of two even wiser students, Rabbi Elazar Hisma and Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda, who had neither bread nor clothing, and resolved to seat them at the head of the academy. When they came only at his second summons, he told them he was granting them not authority but servitude.
02.why: The Gemara has read the verse about King Azariah living in an "independent house" to mean that until then a king is a servant of the people; Rabban Gamliel's words to his appointees illustrate that office is servitude.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader of the academy, traveling on the ship, who appoints the two students.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: His fellow traveler, who brought extra flour and points out the two poor students.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar Ḥisma
people.about: A student said to be able to calculate the drops in the sea, yet without bread or clothing.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda
people.about: The second such student, appointed together with Rabbi Elazar Ḥisma.

terms.meaning: To give them a leading position in the academy, the house of study.

03.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of Yosef ben Eilim of Tzippori, a priest appointed to replace a High Priest who had become temporarily disqualified. Once the disqualification passed and the original High Priest returned, the other priests would not let Yosef ben Eilim serve at all, neither as High Priest nor as an ordinary priest. The Gemara explains: not as High Priest because two equal High Priests would breed enmity, and not as an ordinary priest because one may raise a person in holiness but not lower him.
03.why: The discussion asks what happens to a stand-in High Priest after the original returns; Rabbi Meir says he keeps the High Priest's duties, and Rabbi Yosei cites this incident for his view that the stand-in may serve in neither role.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Yosef ben Eilim
people.about: A priest from Tzippori appointed as substitute High Priest, then barred from serving.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple in Jerusalem, who alone performed certain rites, such as those of Yom Kippur.
Any priest descended from Aaron who served in the Temple without the High Priest's special rank.

04.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the Nasi, saw the academy rise for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan just as for him, and while they were away he set new rules marking his higher rank. Offended, they plotted to unseat him by asking him to teach tractate Uktzin, which he did not know, but Rabbi Ya'akov ben Korshei overheard and recited it aloud behind his room until he learned it; he passed the test and had the two expelled. Readmitted after they kept tossing in notes with questions and answers, they were penalized by having their teachings cited only as "Others" and "Some say." Years later Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son questioned this, and his father then taught a ruling "in the name of Rabbi Meir."
04.why: The Gemara has quoted a teaching on how the academy shows honor to the Nasi, the Hakham and the deputy Nasi; Rabbi Yohanan says it was taught in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's day, and this story tells how those rules came about.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages, who sets the rules of honor and has his rivals expelled.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Hakham of the academy, who plots with Rabbi Natan to unseat the Nasi.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: The deputy Nasi, whose father, the text says, was the Babylonian Exilarch; he later goes to make peace.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Korshei
people.about: A Sage who overhears the plot and quietly helps the Nasi prepare.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's son and successor, who teaches the story's aftermath to his own son.

terms.meaning: The president of the Sages' court and academy, the highest office among the Sages.
Literally "sage"; here a named office in the academy, ranking below the Nasi.
Head of the court, second to the Nasi.
A tractate of the Mishna on the ritual impurity of stalks and peels of produce, known as obscure.

05.note: Rav Yosef was known as "Sinai," a master of vast knowledge, and Rabba as "one who uproots mountains," a sharp reasoner. The Babylonian Sages sent to the Land of Israel asking which should take precedence, and the answer came back that Sinai is preferable, since everyone needs the owner of the wheat. Even so, Rav Yosef declined the post; Rabba led the yeshiva for twenty-two years before Rav Yosef took over, and all that time Rav Yosef would not even have a bloodletter come to his home.
05.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just reported a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis over whether the learned scholar or the incisive one is preferable; the Gemara shows the question deciding a real appointment.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Called "Sinai" for his knowledge; chosen for the post but declined it in deference to Rabba.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Called "one who uproots mountains" for his sharp reasoning; headed the yeshiva for twenty-two years.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study; its head was the leading Sage of the place.
A picture for the scholar who holds the raw material of the tradition, the sources everyone else depends on.
A healer who drew blood, a common treatment at the time; summoning one home was a sign of status.

06.note: Abaye, Rava, Rabbi Zeira and Rabba bar Mattana were studying together and needed someone to head their group. They agreed that whoever made a statement that could not be refuted would lead. Every statement was refuted except Abaye's, and when Rabba saw Abaye lift his head, he said to him: Nahmani, begin and speak.
06.why: The discussion is about which kind of scholar should lead, the learned one or the incisive one; this group settles its leader by a test of sharp argument, and the Gemara goes on to ask which of two of its members is preferable.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The one member of the group whose statement was not refuted; Rabba calls him by his name, Nahmani.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A member of the study group.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A member of the study group.

people.name: Rabba bar Mattana
people.about: A member of the study group.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The Sage who sees Abaye lift his head and invites him to begin.

07.note: Rabbi Tarfon swore on the lives of his sons that he had heard from his teachers a difference between collecting a sacrifice's blood and sprinkling it, but could not remember what it was. Rabbi Akiva said he would explain it: improper intent counts with sprinkling but not with collecting, and the penalties for doing each outside the Temple or by an unfit person differ in the same way. Rabbi Tarfon swore by the Temple service that Rabbi Akiva had not strayed right or left from what he had heard, and said: Akiva, anyone who leaves you is like one who leaves his life.
07.why: The mishna says improper intent while collecting the blood disqualifies an offering; Rabbi Akiva's words here say it does not, and the Gemara raises this contradiction and resolves it right after.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who heard a teaching from his teachers but could not explain it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who works out the explanation on his own, matching what Rabbi Tarfon heard.

terms.meaning: The priest's catching of the animal's blood in a sacred vessel after it is slaughtered, one of the rites of a sacrifice.
The priest's casting of the collected blood against the altar, the central rite of a sacrifice.
A wrong plan in the priest's mind during a rite, such as to eat the offering at the wrong time, which can invalidate it.
Literally "cutting off": a severe punishment from Heaven for certain sins, understood as early death or being cut off from one's people.

08.note: Rav Ashi recounts what Huna bar Natan told him. Huna bar Natan was once standing before Izgadar, king of Persia, with his belt worn too high, and the king lowered it into place, quoting the verse that calls Israel "a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation." When Huna bar Natan told this to Ameimar, Ameimar said that in him the promise "kings shall be your foster fathers" had come true.
08.why: The Gemara has just explained that priests may not gird their belts where the body sweats, neither below the loins nor above the elbows; this incident shows a king correcting a Jew whose belt sat too high.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who passes on the incident he heard from Huna bar Natan.

people.name: Huna bar Natan
people.about: A Jew who stood before the king of Persia; the king straightened his belt.

people.name: Izgadar
people.about: King of Persia, who lowers Huna bar Natan's belt and quotes a verse to him.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage to whom Huna bar Natan tells the incident, and who answers with a verse.

terms.meaning: A phrase from Exodus describing the people of Israel as a whole nation set apart and holy, as priests are among a people.

09.note: In the academy at Yavne the Sages were asked how long a firstborn offering may be eaten; Rabbi Tarfon answered two days and one night, comparing it to peace offerings. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, a student attending for the first time, countered each argument by comparing it instead to sin and guilt offerings, eaten for only one day and night, until Rabbi Akiva stepped in and Rabbi Tarfon withdrew. Rabbi Akiva cited a verse linking it to peace offerings; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili linked it to the thanks offering instead, and Rabbi Akiva then argued from an extra phrase in the verse. When Rabbi Yishmael heard, he sent word to Rabbi Akiva that he had been mistaken to concede, and should have held to his first argument.
09.why: The mishna rules that a firstborn offering is eaten for two days and one night, and a teaching derives it from a verse; this debate shows how the rule was argued out, and the Gemara then explains what divides Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who gives the answer and defends it until he withdraws.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A student in the academy for the first time, who challenges every argument.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who steps into the debate in Rabbi Tarfon's place.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who hears of the debate and sends word that Rabbi Akiva erred.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a kosher animal, given to a priest, sacrificed, and eaten by priests.
A voluntary sacrifice shared between the altar, the priests and the owner; eaten for two days and the night between.
Sacrifices brought to atone for particular sins; the priests eat them within one day and the following night.
A way of reading the Torah: two things placed side by side in a verse are taken to share the same law.

10.note: Rav taught that if the altar is damaged, every sacrifice slaughtered there is disqualified, adding that there is a verse behind this rule but they had forgotten which one. When his disciple Rav Kahana went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he found Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, asking in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, where this very rule comes from. The story as given here stops at that question; it does not say which verse he named.
10.why: This opens a new topic, the damaged altar; once the verse is supplied, the Gemara sets Rav's ruling against Rabbi Yohanan's, who disqualifies even animals not yet slaughtered.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who gives the ruling but has forgotten its verse.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's disciple, who travels from Babylonia to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; Rav Kahana finds him teaching the source of the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Shimon teaches.

terms.meaning: Of a sacrifice: no longer fit to be offered or eaten.

10.flag: The story stops at Rabbi Shimon's question; the verse that answers it, and Rav Kahana's remark that this was the verse Rav forgot, fall in the next segment.

11.note: On the day the crowd pelted with etrogim a Sadducee priest who poured the Sukkot water offering on his feet instead of on the altar, a corner of the altar was damaged in the chaos. The priests brought a lump of salt and sealed the gap. They did this not because it made the altar fit for service again, but so that the altar would not be seen damaged.
11.why: The Gemara asks whether the karkov of the altar, a ledge or engraving, is also essential to it; it answers yes from this teaching, which says an altar without its corner, ramp, base or square shape is unfit, and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda adds the ledge.

terms.meaning: A member of a Second Temple group that rejected the Sages' oral traditions, including the water offering on Sukkot.
On the festival of Sukkot, water was poured on the altar as an offering, a rite based on the Sages' tradition.
A citron, a citrus fruit carried by worshippers during Sukkot.

12.note: There was an oven whose walls and floor had been smeared with animal fat. Rabba bar Ahilai forbade eating bread baked in it forever, even plain bread eaten with salt alone, for fear that someone would eat it with kutah, a dish made with milk. In his view, the oven would never be fully rid of the fat.
12.why: The Gemara has been asking when a vessel that took in the taste of sacred meat must be broken; this ruling on an oven that took in fat is then challenged by a teaching that firing the oven cleanses it, and Rabba bar Ahilai's view is refuted.

people.name: Rabba bar Ahilai
people.about: A Sage who forbids bread from the greased oven forever; elsewhere in the discussion his name is spelled Rava bar Ahilai.

terms.meaning: A dip made from milk, water, salt and bread crumbs; eating meat-tainted bread with it would mix meat and milk, which Jewish law forbids.

13.note: A teaching says a priest must make himself ritually impure to bury a close relative, and if he refuses, others make him impure against his will. It tells of Yosef the priest, whose wife died on the eve of Passover; he did not want to become impure, because he wanted to bring the Passover offering. His fellow priests took a vote and made him impure against his will.
13.why: Abaye has said a mourner's status on the day of the Passover offering depends on whether the death came before or after midday; the Gemara cites this incident and sets it against a teaching about a nazirite to show that very distinction.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest whose wife died on Passover eve; he wanted to stay pure for the offering.

terms.meaning: A religious status, here from contact with the dead, that bars a person from the Temple and from eating sacrifices until purified.
The Passover lamb, slaughtered on the afternoon before Passover and eaten that night; only the ritually pure may eat it.
A commandment, a religious duty.

14.note: Rava passes on a story that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, told as an argument. A priest who had immersed that day, and so would be pure only at nightfall, asked the priest handing out the sacrificial food for a share of a meal offering to eat that evening. The serving priest refused with an argument from a lighter case to a stricter one; the immersed priest turned the argument around, and the serving priest settled it with a verse: the portion belongs to the priest who offers it, so come offer and eat. The same exchange repeated over a sin offering and then the breast and thigh of a peace offering, and the immersed priest left with his arguments on his head, a mourner on his right and a priest awaiting atonement on his left.
14.why: The mishna says a priest who immersed that day, a mourner, and one still owed an atonement offering get no share of the sacrifices even to eat that evening; Rava says he learned this rule from this story, and Rav Ahai then asks why it leaves out the firstborn offering.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who says he learned the rule from this story.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who told the story as a way of arguing the rule.

terms.meaning: A person who has bathed in a ritual bath to end impurity but stays impure until sunset of that day.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.
A person on the day a close relative dies, who may not take part in sacrifices.
A sacrifice certain people must bring to finish their purification before they may eat sacred food.

15.note: Once human bones were found in the Chamber of the Woodshed in the Temple, and the Sages wanted to decree impurity on all of Jerusalem, out of concern that there were lost graves elsewhere in the city. Rabbi Yehoshua stood up and said: Is it not a shame and disgrace for us to decree impurity on the city of our fathers? Where are the dead of the flood, and where are the dead killed by Nebuchadnezzar? The text here does not say what the Sages then decided.
15.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish disagree over whether the flood reached the Land of Israel and left hidden graves there; Rabbi Yohanan cites Rabbi Yehoshua's words against Reish Lakish, and the Gemara debates what they prove.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who stands up to oppose declaring Jerusalem impure.

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar
people.about: Named by Rabbi Yehoshua: the conqueror whose killings left dead in the land.

terms.meaning: To rule that everyone entering a place is treated as ritually impure, as if they had touched a corpse, barring them from the Temple and sacred food.
A room in the Temple courtyard where wood for the altar was stored and checked.
The flood of Noah's time, whose victims some Sages feared lay in unknown graves.

16.note: Ifera Hurmiz, the mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent an offering to Rava with the message: sacrifice this for me, for the sake of Heaven. Rava told Rav Safra and Rav Aha bar Huna to take two gentile youths of the same age, find a spot where the sea had just thrown up fresh silt, where no one had yet been, and take new wood and bring out fire from new vessels. The two youths would then offer the sacrifice for her, for the sake of Heaven.
16.why: The Gemara has ruled that gentiles may offer sacrifices anywhere, that a Jew may not help them do it, but that he may instruct them how; Rava's instructions, carried out by gentile youths, illustrate this. Abaye then asks whose view the new wood follows.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: The mother of King Shapur of Persia, who sends Rava an offering.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who gives instructions for her offering.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: One of the two Sages Rava sends to arrange the sacrifice.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Huna
people.about: The other Sage Rava sends with Rav Safra.

terms.meaning: Offered to God, with a sincere religious purpose.
A person who is not Jewish.

17.note: Avimi, Rav Hisda's teacher, had forgotten tractate Menahot, so he went to his own student Rav Hisda to relearn it, thinking that making the effort to travel would help him remember. On his way back, Rav Nahman met him and asked how a priest removes a handful from a meal offering; Avimi pointed to a vessel on the ground. Asked whether one may use a vessel resting on the ground, Avimi said a priest would first lift it, and he answered the same about placing the offering in a vessel. When Rav Nahman objected that this needs three priests, Avimi replied: let it need thirteen, like the daily offering.
17.why: Rabbi Zeira has said the question whether a vessel resting on the ground can be used for a meal offering arose when Avimi studied at Rav Hisda's; the Gemara first asks how a teacher came to study with his student, then gives the exchange.

people.name: Avimi
people.about: Rav Hisda's teacher, who forgot a tractate and relearned it from his student.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Avimi's student, who says Avimi once gave him many blows of mockery over a ruling.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who meets Avimi and questions him about meal offerings.

terms.meaning: A Temple offering of flour, often with oil and frankincense; a handful is burned on the altar and the rest eaten by priests.
The rite in which a priest scoops a handful of the meal offering to burn on the altar.
Here, placing the offering in a sacred Temple vessel, which makes it holy for the service.
The lamb offered every morning and afternoon in the Temple, whose service involved thirteen priests.

18.note: A man sowed seeds in someone else's vineyard while the grapes on the vines were just budding. The case came before the Sages, who ruled the seeds forbidden, because of the ban on growing mixed crops in a vineyard, but left the vines permitted.
18.why: Rav has ruled that a thanks offering's loaves can be disqualified though the offering is not; the Gemara asks why an argument from lighter to weightier does not spare the loaves, since this ruling seems to reject such an argument, then rejects the comparison.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the mixed produce becomes forbidden for any use.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.

19.note: A man sowed seeds in his friend's vineyard while the grapes on the vines were just budding. The case came before the Sages, who ruled the seeds forbidden, because of the ban on growing mixed crops in a vineyard, but left the vines permitted.
19.why: In a second version of Rabbi Elazar's question, about the Shavuot lambs and loaves, Rav rules the loaves can be disqualified though the lambs are not; the Gemara challenges this with the vineyard ruling, which seems to reject such an argument, then answers it.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on sowing other crops in a vineyard; the mixed produce becomes forbidden for any use.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.

19.flag: Same vineyard incident as Menachot 15a-b (A920BB), cited again in shortened form, with "etc.", in the Gemara's alternate version of the discussion.

20.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells how he went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and found Yosef the Babylonian there, who loved every ruling he heard. Yosef asked whether an offering slaughtered with the intent to leave some of its blood until the next day is fit; Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua said it was fit, and Yosef asked again that evening, the next morning, at noon and in the afternoon, until Rabbi Elazar added that Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit, and Yosef's face lit up. Yosef explained that Rabbi Yehuda had taught him it was unfit, and none of Rabbi Yehuda's other disciples had heard it; now his lost teaching was restored. Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua wept, praised scholars who love Torah, and said that Rabbi Yehuda learned this through his father from Rabbi Eliezer.
20.why: The Gemara has said that in Rabbi Yehuda's view everyone agrees intent to leave the blood until the next day disqualifies an offering; it cites this account to challenge that, then works out what Rabbi Yehuda actually taught Yosef.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The Sage who tells the story of his visit to Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
people.about: The teacher Yosef questions again and again; he weeps at Yosef's love of Torah.

people.name: Yosef the Babylonian
people.about: A student who had learned a ruling from Rabbi Yehuda that no one else seemed to know.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Yosef's earlier teacher; son of Rabbi Elai, who was a student of Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who held the offering unfit, the source of Rabbi Yehuda's teaching.

terms.meaning: Of a sacrifice: valid, properly offered and acceptable.
What the priest has in mind while slaughtering; a wrong plan, such as delaying the blood rites past their time, can disqualify an offering.
Here, a teaching as passed down from a particular Sage.
